newsitem.title: USA: Rep. Leach sees damage from Comptroller coffee.
newsitem.headline: Rep. Leach sees damage from Comptroller coffee.

text.p: Comptroller of the Currency Eugene Ludwig may have harmed his chances for becoming the primary financial services regulator in the future by attending a White House fundraising event, House Banking Committee Chairman Jim Leach said Tuesday.
Leach criticized the comptroller for attending a coffee at the White House with bank industry officials sponsored by the Democratic National Committee.
"It's unclear whether that's an issue that's been exagerrated or understated," the Iowa Republican said at a meeting of the Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers here.
"I personally think it's unseemly," Leach added.

Leach said Ludwig's involvement would help make the case that the Federal Reserve rather than the OCC, a part of the executive branch, should be the primary regulator of financial services companies in any reform that is enacted.
"I think it raises some implications for this question of who becomes the ultimate regulator," Leach said. The question raised is "whether one wants to have a politicized regulatory system."
The controvery could also add to pressure for campaign finance reform, but Leach did not sound optimistic.

"This comptroller meeting is very small potatoes relative to the S & L (savings and loan) debacle, which I thought was the greatest cause celebre we could ever have for campaign finance reform, and it did not materialize," Leach said.
Leach also reiterated his longstanding opposition to proposals that would allow common ownership of financial and nonfinancial companies.
"I have very grave doubts," Leach said. Mergers of companies like General Motors Corp and Citicorp would be "a fairly nutty circumstance."
Leach said he had met recently with Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin to discuss the issue.
"Differences of opinion were made known," Leach said. "It was my impression that the Treasury has not made a final judgment."

On another contentious issue, Leach said he has made no judgments on possible legislation to expand credit union membership. Membership in the tax-exempt cooperatives has been sharply limited by a federal court in Washington, but the credit union industry plans to go to Congress to overturn the limits if an appeal to the Supreme Court fails. (Aaron Pressman, 202-898-8312)
